The DPPH• radical-scavenging activity was determined according to a previously reported method with slight modifications [52]. Briefly, the PSMH solutions were diluted to 0.05 mg/mL and mixed with a 40 μg/mL DPPH• solution at a ratio of 1:2 (v/v). The mixture was incubated in the dark at room temperature for 30 min. After incubation, the absorbance was measured at 517 nm using a UV–Vis spectrophotometer (L5S; INESA Analytical Instrument Co., Ltd., Shanghai, China). The DPPH• radical-scavenging rate (%) was calculated using the following formula:(5)DPPH• radical-scavenging rate (%) = 1−A1−A2A0×100 where A1 is the absorbance of the sample with DPPH• solution; A2 is the sample’s background absorbance without DPPH• solution; and A0 is the absorbance of the DPPH• solution with deionized water (blank).
The ABTS•+ radical-scavenging activity was evaluated based on a previously reported method with slight modifications [53]. Briefly, the PSMH solutions were diluted to 0.05 mg/mL and mixed with the ABTS•+ working solution at a ratio of 1:3 (v/v). The mixture was incubated in the dark at room temperature for 6 min, after which the absorbance was measured at 734 nm using a UV-Vis spectrophotometer. The ABTS•+ radical-scavenging rate (%) was calculated using the following formula:(6)ABTS•+ radical-scavenging rate (%) = 1−A1−A2A0×100 where A1 is the absorbance of the sample with ABTS•+ solution; A2 is the sample’s background absorbance without ABTS•+ solution; and A0 is the absorbance of the ABTS•+ solution with deionized water (blank).
The peptidomic analysis of the optimized PSMH was performed using nano-LC–MS/MS according to a previously established method [54]. Briefly, the analysis was carried out on an Ultimate 3000 system coupled to a Q ExactiveTM Hybrid Quadrupole-OrbitrapTM mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). The acquired raw data were processed using Byonic software (version 4.2.4; Protein Metrics Inc., Cupertino, CA, USA).
The potential bioactivity of peptides identified from PSMH was initially evaluated using PeptideRanker, an online bioactive peptide prediction tool (http://distilldeep.ucd.ie/PeptideRanker/ (accessed on 22 November 2025)) [55]. This tool employs a machine learning algorithm to assign a score ranging from 0 to 1 to each peptide sequence, thereby reflecting its probability of exhibiting bioactivity. In this study, peptides with PeptideRanker scores greater than 0.5 were considered potentially bioactive and selected for further analysis.
The water solubility of the selected peptides was subsequently evaluated using the Peptide Property Calculator (http://www.innovagen.com/proteomics-tools (accessed on 22 November 2025)). Meanwhile, key physicochemical properties, including molecular weight, isoelectric point (pI), and net charge at physiological pH (7.0), were also calculated to provide a comprehensive assessment of peptide characteristics. The peptides with both potential bioactivity and good water solubility were then subjected to molecular docking analysis.
Molecular docking was performed to investigate the interactions between the selected peptides and representative antioxidant targets, including the free radicals ABTS (ABTS•+) and DPPH (DPPH•), as well as the key target protein Keap1 in the Keap1–Nrf2 pathway. These targets were selected to represent direct radical-scavenging mechanisms and protein-mediated antioxidant pathways, respectively. The 3D structures of the peptides were constructed using PyMOL (version 3.1.0; Schrödinger, LLC, New York, NY, USA) and saved in MOL2 format. Subsequently, the peptide structures were prepared for docking using AutoDock Tools (version 4.2.6; The Scripps Research Institute, La Jolla, CA, USA), which involved the addition of hydrogen atoms and the definition of torsion trees to allow all rotatable bonds to rotate freely. The conformation and interactions of the complex were visualized using PyMOL and Discovery Studio Visualizer (version 17.2.0; Dassault Systèmes BIOVIA, San Diego, CA, USA) based on the docking pose with the lowest binding energy.
MD simulations were performed using YASARA Dynamics (version 14.10.5; YASARA Biosciences GmbH, Vienna, Austria) for 100 ns on the following systems: the WQFR–Keap1 complex, the FRF–Keap1 complex, the FEFR–Keap1 complex, the RWL–Keap1 complex, and unbound Keap1 as a blank control. For each complex, the initial structure for MD simulation was selected as the lowest-energy binding conformation obtained from molecular docking. All MD simulations were carried out following the protocol previously established by our group [35]. Briefly, MD simulations were conducted using the AMBER14 force field. The system was solvated in a simulation cell with periodic boundary conditions, utilizing the TIP3P explicit water model. To mimic physiological conditions, an ion concentration of 0.9% NaCl was maintained. The system was neutralized by replacing water molecules with counter-ions at positions of maximum or minimum electrostatic potential. After the simulations, trajectory analyses were conducted to evaluate the root mean square deviation (RMSD), root mean square fluctuation (RMSF), radius of gyration (Rg), and solvent-accessible surface area (SASA), which collectively reflect the structural stability, flexibility, compactness, and solvent exposure of the systems during the simulation period.
The selected peptides were synthesized by solid-phase peptide synthesis at Sangon Biotech Co., Ltd. (Shanghai, China). All peptides were purified to a minimum purity of 98%. Peptide identity and purity were confirmed by high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) coupled with mass spectrometry (MS) prior to biological activity evaluation (Supplementary Figure S2).
HepG2 cells were cultured in DMEM supplemented with 4.0 mmol/L L-glutamine, 4.5 g/L glucose, 10% (v/v) FBS, and 1% penicillin–streptomycin, and maintained at 37 °C in a humidified atmosphere containing 5% CO2. The culture medium was refreshed daily. Cells at approximately 80–90% confluence were detached for subsequent experiments using trypsin–EDTA.
The cytotoxic effects of the selected peptides on HepG2 cells were evaluated using the MTT assay, following the previously described method [56]. Briefly, HepG2 cells were seeded into 96-well plates at a density of 1 × 104 cells/well and incubated for 24 h to allow attachment. Following incubation, the medium was replaced with fresh DMEM containing various concentrations of the selected peptides, and the cells were incubated for an additional 24 h. Subsequently, 20 μL of MTT solution (5 mg/mL in PBS) was added to each well and incubated for 4 h to facilitate the formation of formazan crystals. After discarding the supernatant carefully, the resulting formazan crystals were dissolved in 150 μL of DMSO. Finally, the absorbance was measured at 490 nm using a microplate reader (Spark 10M; Tecan, Männedorf, Switzerland). Cell viability was calculated based on the equation below:(7)Cell viability%=Asample−AblankAcontrol−Ablank×100 where Asample represents the absorbance of the well containing cells treated with the peptides, Acontrol represents the absorbance of the well containing untreated control cells, and Ablank represents the absorbance of the well containing only culture medium without cells.
HepG2 cells were seeded into 96-well plates at a density of 1 × 104 cells/well and incubated for 12 h to allow attachment. Subsequently, the medium was replaced with fresh DMEM containing various concentrations of the selected peptides, and the cells were then incubated for another 24 h to assess their potential protective effects against oxidative stress. Following peptide pretreatment, the medium was replaced with fresh DMEM containing 500 μM H2O2, and the cells were incubated for an additional 12 h to induce oxidative stress. The concentration of H2O2 (500 μM) was selected based on preliminary experiments, which demonstrated that this concentration reduced cell viability to approximately 50%, thereby enabling the establishment of a reproducible oxidative stress model suitable for evaluating cytoprotective effects. After exposure to H2O2, cell viability was determined using the MTT assay as described above. The relative cell viability was calculated based on the following equation:(8)Cell viability %=Asample−AblankAcontrol−Ablank×100 where Asample represents the absorbance of the well containing cells treated with the peptides, Acontrol represents the absorbance of the well containing untreated control cells, and Ablank represents the absorbance of the well containing only culture medium without cells.
The activities of antioxidant enzymes, including SOD, CAT, and GSH-Px, were determined in this study. Briefly, the HepG2 cells were treated with the selected peptides and subsequently exposed to H2O2 to induce oxidative stress, as described above. Following treatment, the cells were washed twice with pre-cooled PBS, lysed using RIPA buffer on ice, and then centrifuged at 14,000× g for 10 min at 4 °C. The supernatant was collected for subsequent analyses. Total protein content in the cell lysates was determined using a BCA protein assay kit to normalize enzyme activities across samples. The activities of SOD, CAT, and GSH-Px were determined using commercial assay kits according to the manufacturer’s instructions and expressed relative to the total protein content.
All experiments in this study were conducted in triplicate (n = 3), and the results were expressed as mean ± standard deviation (SD). Statistical significance was determined using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA), followed by Duncan’s multiple range test, with p < 0.05 considered statistically significant.

Subsequently, 20 μL of MTT solution (5 mg/mL in PBS) was added to each well and incubated for 4 h to facilitate the formation of formazan crystals. 4 conclusions: This study systematically demonstrated that peony seed meal, an abundant agricultural by-product, can serve as a valuable source of potent antioxidant peptides. By integrating ANN-based process optimization with high-resolution peptidomics and multi-level bioactivity evaluation, an efficient and reliable strategy for peptide discovery has been established. Neutrase-mediated hydrolysis optimized through the BP-ANN model significantly enhanced antioxidant activity, outperforming many previously reported protein hydrolysates. The optimized process preferentially generated low molecular weight peptides, which are structurally favorable for antioxidant function. In silico analyses revealed strong binding affinities of selected peptides toward both free radicals and the Keap1 protein, suggesting dual antioxidant mechanisms involving direct radical scavenging and modulation of the Keap1–Nrf2 signaling pathway. Among the screened peptides, FRF exhibited the most pronounced residue-specific interaction within the Keap1 Kelch domain and showed superior cytoprotective effects in HepG2 cells. Both FRF and RWL effectively restored intracellular antioxidant enzyme activities under oxidative stress, confirming their biological relevance beyond chemical assays. Overall, this work provides mechanistic insight into the antioxidant action of PSM-derived peptides and proposes an integrated discovery framework that bridges intelligent hydrolysis optimization, in silico prediction, and cellular validation. These findings support the sustainable conversion of peony seed meal into high-value functional food ingredients with potential applications in health-promoting formulations.
